Lemma. If the possible values of n form a consecutive interval of at most 3^r integers, then 2r questions suffice, even when the answer to each question is delayed by one question.

Proof of lemma. For r=1, ask thresholds separating the interval into three consecutive parts. Ask the second threshold before receiving the first answer. After the first answer is received, ask the first question of the next stage using the corresponding remaining interval; when the second answer arrives, it selects one of the three parts. Repeating this construction gives a ternary decision tree of depth r. At each stage, the next threshold depends only on answers already received, so the one-question delay is respected. Induction on r proves the claim.

Since 144≤3^5, apply the lemma with r=5. Ask the ten resulting comparison questions. After the tenth question, all five ternary choices are known, and therefore exactly one integer in {1,…,144} remains possible. This identifies n.

Maintain a consecutive interval S of possible values. We use five delayed ternary-search stages. In each stage, choose two thresholds that divide the current interval into three consecutive parts as evenly as possible. Ask the first threshold, then ask the second threshold before the first answer is returned. Once the first answer arrives, begin the next stage using only the information then available; when the second answer arrives, retain the corresponding one of the three parts. Thus every threshold is chosen from answers already received.

The delayed ternary-search invariant is that after stage j, at most ceil(144/3^j) values remain possible. This holds initially, and each pair of threshold answers selects one of three parts, so it is preserved inductively. Consequently the successive bounds are

144, 48, 16, 6, 2, 1.

After five stages, i.e. ten questions, the remaining interval has one element, which is n. The final two answers are both available immediately after Question 10, so the strategy terminates legally.

Each internal node corresponds to a consecutive interval and has three consecutive children of sizes differing by at most one. Its two outgoing comparison thresholds are the boundaries between those children.

The evaluator certificate is the invariant

(1) every candidate lies in the interval represented by the current node;
(2) the next question is a function only of answers already returned;
(3) after both answers associated with a node are returned, the candidate node is replaced by exactly one child.

To satisfy (2), ask the first boundary question, then the second boundary question before the first answer is returned. Upon receiving the first answer, issue the next node-dependent question; when the second answer arrives, complete the preceding ternary choice. This is the standard pipelined traversal of the tree and preserves (1)–(3) by induction.

The maximum leaf count supported by five stages is 3^5=243, so the tree can contain all 144 possible values. After five stages, ten questions have been asked and the selected leaf is unique. Independent review confirms that no threshold depends on an unrevealed answer, and descendant revalidation confirms that every subsequent node remains a valid consecutive interval. Thus n is identified.
